newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore to ignore criticism of libel decision.
newsitem.headline: Singapore to ignore criticism of libel decision.

text.p: If history is any guide, Singapore will shrug off criticism over record damages awarded its leadership in libel suits against a political opponent.
First, Singapore leaders have already said they consider attacks on the suits unjustified.

Second, the bottom line for Singapore is just that, the bottom line. Previous criticism of Singapore's political and legal system has never stopped multi-national companies and investors from pouring in billions of dollars.

In the past, human rights groups and some countries like the United States have blasted Singapore over what they viewed as draconian punishments, limits on individual rights, and restrictions on the opposition.
But more than 2,000 major multi-nationals have set up regional headquarters on the island, and investment has steadily grown despite such attacks.

The current flap centres around a Singapore court award on Thursday to Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and 10 senior members of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) of a record S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in libel damages.

They were suing Tang Liang Hong, who branded them liars during a general election campaign after they had called him an "anti-Christian Chinese chauvinist" endangering racial harmony. A member of Hong Kong's Bar Council said the award seemed "very large" compared with cases in Hong Kong or Britain -- which share a Common Law-based legal system with Singapore.

"The English courts have said that when you get to such record amounts of damages you're beginning to put curbs on freedom of expression because it will have a chilling effect," said Philip Dykes of the council.
"In Taiwan you can pretty much say anything against the government and get away with it," said Chang Lin-chen, a law professor at National Taiwan University.

"It gives Singapore's critics in the U.S. added ammunition," analyst Bruce Gale of the Political & Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC) told Reuters, saying Singapore was likely to continue to be dogged with an authoritarian image in America.
But Singapore leaders have said they had to bring the suits to defend their integrity and ability to govern effectively.

The court agreed, finding various of Tang's comments amounted to suggesting the PAP leaders had committed criminal conspiracy and criminal defamation. "It affects their moral authority to govern," Justice Chao Hick Tin said.
Stable government has been a key talking point for Singapore in selling the island to international investors.

The political stability offered by the PAP, which has ruled Singapore since 1959, provides certainty and eliminates risk. Corporations can plan five, 10, even 15 years in the future knowing little will change.
The monolithic PAP has never hesitated to take legal action against opponents when it felt it was justified.

"Opposition politicians in Singapore regularly find themselves in legal trouble," one Singapore ambassador recently wrote. "The reason is they often make reckless, defamatory statements...which they are unable to justify in court."
The opposition won just two seats in January's general election to the PAP's 81, ensuring its pro-business policies will remain in place.

Those include low corporate taxation, minimal interference in foreign enterprises, low inflation and a strong, stable currency, which have helped make Singapore one of the world's most prosperous nations in terms of growth and average income.
But not everyone thinks the good times will go on indefinitely.

"Up to a certain stage you can separate economic reform from political reform, but we have come to a stage where political reform is a precondition for sustaining economic growth," one economist said.

Singapore has been hearing warnings about how economic prosperity must eventually be coupled with political liberalism for decades now, with little evidence from its own experience that they are justified.

Until such hard evidence emerges, dramatic changes in policy are unlikely by a government that saw the general election as having, in Goh's words, "rejected Western-style liberal democracy and freedoms, putting individual rights over that of society".
In the first quarter of 1997, new manufacturing investment commitments to Singapore amounted to S$2.2 billion, up 66 percent from a year earlier.
